To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use.

We develop a one-parameter family of Jordanian twists by extending the method used for classical and classical modified twists. Applying the one-parameter Jordanian twist Angeles and Kurose constructed a quantum affine Lie group, thus we provide a new perspective on their construction. Furthermore, we calculate the classical r-form Jordanian limit of our twist framework, resulting in a Godement subregular Poisson Lie group structure.

This study has two primary objectives. The first is to extend regular expressions with the NOT and XOR operators, which in many cases can be processed using Buechi automata. We have developed a new approach based on saturation solving, utilizing a solver that can handle disjunctions, and proved it is equivalent to Buechi automata solving. The second objective is to adapt this method for the purpose of verifying safety properties in syndesys, a real-time safety controller synthesizer, which now supports NOT and XOR operators within regular expressions.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive understanding of the structure of conformal block operators in CFT$_2, combined with spinning primary fields. The key to our approach lies in the detailed explanation of conformal invariant quantities, particularly the way massless fields transform under the conformal group. We then outline how this information is used to define conformal block operators for both integer and half-integer spin primary fields. Furthermore, we elaborate on the relationship between (1,1)-CFT$_2 and the AdS$_3$ gravity, incorporating spinning primary fields into the picture. In the process, we provide a precise map between spinning CFT primary fields and massive AdS$_3$ fields, taking into account both their properties and behavior.

To achieve high sensitivity in wide-field X-ray monitoring systems like those intended for gravitational wave event follow-up, the issue of simultaneously imaging multiple areas of the sky on a single detector must be addressed. A configuration utilizing a lobster-eye (also known as a wide-field optic) in front of a sensitive, pointed X-ray telescope like eROSITA is proposed here to resolve this problem. By intentionally designing the field of view of the wide-field optic to be larger than the pointing footprint of a single satellite, multiple areas can be imaged on a single detector, allowing for a significant increase in the system's overall sensitivity without the need for a more complex, multifocal design. A simulation demonstrating the effectiveness of this strategy by detecting a signal within the desired sensitivity level for a given system is presented in the paper.

The halo model of structure formation is a powerful tool for understanding the connection between gravity, dark matter, and observable phenomena. A key component of this model is the halo mass function, which describes the distribution of halos across a range of masses. However, computing the mass function accurately is challenging due to the role of velocity field in initial conditions, which is difficult to determine from observational data. Despite the velocity field's influence on the formation and evolution of halos, its impact on the mass function is not well understood. This study uses the halo structure function, which incorporates the velocity field, and maps it onto the linear power spectrum. Analyzing $N$-body simulations, we found that the halo bias and mass function are unaffected by the second derivative of the velocity field. As a result, we can replace the velocity field with the growing mode of the density perturbation without significant loss of accuracy. This finding enables the use of observable quantities, such as Lyman-$\alpha$ forest data, to determine the velocity field's influence on the mass function. Furthermore, we found that the velocity field's impact is negligible compared to the nonlinearities encoded in the halo bias and mass function. This research paves the way for future studies that aim to constrain the halo mass function with observational data.

This study proposes a novel method that combines atomic interferometry with the Meissner effect of a superconducting material to precisely measure tiny changes in local magnetic fields. Unlike conventional atomic interferometry, this approach is not affected by the overall magnetic field or its uniformity, thereby enabling the measurement of both the field's oscillations over time and its spatial distribution. To demonstrate the method's effectiveness, we conducted an experiment using a atomic interferometry system consisting of two atomic beams that intersected above a superconducting YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{7-δ}$ (YBCO) slab and measured the local magnetic field's oscillations as it entered the region near the slab's surface. The results showed that the method could precisely measure both the phase difference between atomic waves and the local magnetic field's decay length above the YBCO slab with a sensitivity of around $10^{-12}$ Tesla.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn clusters on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a single-layer Mn cluster, good agreement with experimental data regarding YSR state splitting was found. However, for a bilayer cluster, spin-orbit coupling became more significant, leading to YSR state splitting that couldn't be accounted for by the local exchange field alone. Reversal field curves for both cluster configurations showed accurate theoretical matches with experimental YSR state splitting patterns.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context, cross-section calculations for weak boson collisions are simplified by utilizing the distribution of colliding lepton energies rather than their actual scattering processes. A key aspect of this method is the use of collinear approximation for W and Z particle decays, which is re-evaluated to meet the requirements of radiative cross-section calculations at second order. A universal characteristic of weak boson colliders is identified, where the most significant contribution to cross-section calculations originates from the nearest, most probable weak boson decays around the center of the colliding lepton spectrum. A straightforward, second-order cross-section calculation is provided for a given process, involving two weak boson collision objects, which can further decay into various lepton pairs. A numerical example is given, demonstrating the efficiency of this approach by applying it to a specific process involving a muon collider and two Z' particles. A formula is offered for determining the relevant weak boson distribution functions, which are found to be identical for W and Z particles due to their similar properties and behavior in high-energy environments.

We bring together Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser in the same venue to address a longstanding issue in semantics. Our gathering focuses on the concept of a sound mirror reflection, which some authors have utilized, while others, including the mentioned logicians, use a near but slightly modified version called a truth mirror reflection. We examine the differences between these two concepts, drawing on the authors' previous work and adding novel insights. Godel's first incompleteness theorem is based on a soundness assumption that is not always met, leading to a re-examination of its proof. We also explore the relationship between mirror reflections and a famous result by Tarski concerning definability. Furthermore, we delve into the connection between the concepts and the Church-Fock theorem.

This paper examines the concept of invariant sets within dynamical systems, with a focus on the definition provided by Shoshillero et al. [12]. We offer an alternative, more intuitive definition emphasizing the preservation of surface characteristics in physical systems. This revised definition serves as the foundation for our main theorem, which states that in a physical system defined by a partial differential equation, only unbounded or constant invariant surfaces exist.

This study tackles the structural acoustic inverse problem where we aim to determine the source sound pressure by measuring the vibration of a structure and sound pressure in an adjacent cavity. A Gaussian process regression-based neural network was employed to solve this problem, dubbed the "GPN solver". The solver was tested on a demo example featuring a clamped rectangular plate connected to a sound cavity. A synthetic data curve was utilized to test the solver's performance when the initial guess matches the true source signal. When the initial guess was distorted, random noise was added to further challenge the solver. In the demo example, the source signal was highly complex, consisting of a harmonic series with multiple frequencies. The GPN solver was able to accurately reconstruct the source signal when the initial guess was precise, but difficulties arose when the initial guess was poorly defined, even with the addition of noise to the vibration and sound pressure data.

Within the easiest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the radiative neutrino oscillation processes into the sector responsible for dark matter, we address both neutrino mass hierarchies and the dark matter relic abundance within a unified framework. Utilizing a two-loop calculation, we evaluate the stability of the vacuum state and reconcile it with the reliability of perturbative approaches. Based on a two-parameter setup (excluding the dark matter mass), we determine the feasible range for neutrino oscillation lengths and the dark matter annihilation cross-section, meeting the experimental neutrino constraints and satisfying the dark matter relic abundance requirements. Furthermore, we verify that the easiest scoto-seesaw model accommodates the observed dark matter properties, neutrino oscillation lengths, and the 125 GeV Higgs boson mass, while also ensuring the stability of the vacuum state.
